source.title: ALL-FEM: Agentic Large Language models Fine-tuned for Finite Element Methods
source.authors: Rushikesh Deotale; A. Srinivasan; Mahmoud Golestanian; Yuan Tian; Tianyi Zhang; P. Vlachos; Hector Gomez

record.tranche_reason: The study compares downstream benchmark performance across models of different sizes, a different measure and setting from pretraining-loss scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper cites scaling-law work and says its fine-tuning validation results are consistent with it, but does not measure held-out pretraining loss across parameter, token, or compute sweeps. Those citations and fine-tuning training-loss curves are not results for V1 or V2. The reported FEM benchmark scores bear on V6. Figure-only breakdowns without accessible values in the supplied text are not transcribed as rows.
record.test_reason: An application paper (FEniCS code generation) that compares a few off-the-shelf and fine-tuned models of different total sizes on a 39-problem downstream benchmark. It reports size ordering in accuracy, which bears weakly on V6 in a new setting. Size is confounded with model family, MoE versus dense architecture and reasoning mode. No loss or compute sweep and no fitted scale–performance relation are reported, so it does not bear on V1–V5 or V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that larger models perform better in the two-agent framework, and that fine-tuning and agentic orchestration further improve correctness. They also conclude that a fine-tuned GPT-OSS 120B agentic system beats non-agentic GPT-5 Thinking, so smaller fine-tuned models can rival much larger ones. The 'consistent with scaling laws' remark refers to fine-tuning token accuracy, not benchmark accuracy.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates supervised, domain-specific LoRA/QLoRA fine-tuning and downstream FEM-code benchmark accuracy, rather than pretraining sweeps of held-out cross-entropy across model size, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with model size, model/family, fine-tuning status, benchmark difficulty and physics category, and deployment setup (two-agent versus non-agentic GPT-5 comparison).
record.peer_reviewed: Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering
record.problems: The benchmark contains 39 problems and the reported comparisons involve different model families and training conditions, so parameter count is not isolated. No uncertainty estimates or fitted scale-performance relationship are reported. The paper notes limitations in its solution-comparison evaluation protocol and benchmark scope.
record.rows_left_out: Difficulty/category plots and other plotted breakdowns were not entered where the supplied text did not expose their numerical values. Fine-tuning validation token accuracy and training-loss trajectories were left out because they are not held-out pretraining-loss scaling measurements.

untested.parts: All: no pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
All: no shape sweep at fixed parameter count.
All: fine-tuning token-accuracy ordering is reported, but no power-law form is fitted.
Predictability: no fitted or calibrated relation to scale or pretraining loss, and only 3–4 models. No within-family size sweep.

missing.what: Fine-tuned Qwen 3 32B outperforms the larger base Llama 3.3 70B. Fine-tuning gains for Llama 70B go from 0 to 8 problems solved.
missing.locator: Section 3.2, 'Fine-tuning Improves Performance in a Two-agent Framework'

missing.what: GPT-OSS 120B activates only ~5.1B parameters per token, which matters for reading 'size' in r4 and r7.
Per-difficulty and per-category counts for base GPT-OSS 120B and the other models are plotted only.

record.verdict_notes: This is a weak V6 test: an application paper with 3–4 models from different families, no uncertainty estimates, and 39 problems. The record's per-row observed/partial/absent states misread point values as effect strengths. The Llama 70B category counts in r15–r17 likely belong to the FT model. The GPT-5 comparison (r18) is a method comparison, not scaling evidence.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, and compute.
Whether fits from small pretraining runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law scaling in other modalities or training regimes.

The study tests FEM-code benchmark performance across selected model sizes, not a calibrated prediction from pretraining loss or a fitted scale-performance law; it does not establish predictability across other downstream tasks.
Dependence of scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations on fitting choices, and systematic bending of scaling curves.

rows.subject: GPT-5 Thinking
rows.size_stated: Exact parameter count not disclosed; estimates are described as well over 1 trillion.
rows.operation_detail: Compared a non-agentic deployment using two zero-shot attempts against the two-agent fine-tuned GPT-OSS deployment.
rows.baseline: GPT-OSS FT in the two-agent framework
rows.value: GPT-OSS FT performs better across all difficulty levels.
rows.locator: Section 3.2, “GPT-OSS FT in a Two-agent Framework Outperforms a non-agentic GPT-5 Thinking Deployment”
rows.note: No numerical GPT-5 score is stated in this passage; model size and fine-tuning/deployment also differ.
rows.check: Compares the study's own method (two-agent FT system) against a non-agentic GPT-5 deployment. Deployment, fine-tuning and family all differ, and GPT-5's size is undisclosed. This is a method comparison, not a scaling result.

relationships.condition: Two-agent FEM benchmark, ordering by total parameter count within the base set (3B, 70B, 120B) and the FT set (3B, 32B, 70B, 120B)
relationships.reason: Accuracy rises monotonically with total parameters in both sets: 0, 0, 58.97% and 0, 12.82%, 20.51%, 71.79% (r1–r7).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy increased from 0%→0%→58.97% in the base series and 0%→12.82%→20.51%→71.79% in the fine-tuned series.

relationships.condition: Same comparisons, when size is taken as the cause and the trend as predictable
relationships.reason: Size is confounded with family, MoE (GPT-OSS ~5.1B active parameters) and reasoning mode. Gains appear as zero-to-nonzero cliffs on medium and hard problems (r8–r11). Fine-tuned Qwen 32B beats base Llama 70B (text), so fine-tuning can outweigh size.
relationships.display_finding: Fine-tuned Qwen 32B beat base Llama 70B, medium and hard problems showed abrupt zero-to-nonzero gains, and comparisons also varied family, reasoning mode and GPT-OSS's approximately 5.1B active parameters.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: The reported two-agent comparisons across model sizes on the 39-problem FEM benchmark
reader_labels.reason: Reported accuracy is higher for the larger models in the tested comparisons, including the fine-tuned 32B, 70B, and 120B models (r1-r7).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Difficulty and physics-category results, and comparison with GPT-5 Thinking
reader_labels.reason: Some fine-tuned models solve no medium or hard problems; category results vary, and the much larger GPT-5 Thinking comparator performs worse than fine-tuned GPT-OSS, so results do not establish a universal or calibrated scale-performance rule (r8-r18).
